claim: Using Welch's Student's t-test against a random-sampling baseline, none of DARTS, NAO, or ENAS significantly outperforms random sampling in the RNN (PTB) search space, and NAO is significantly WORSE than random sampling (p=0.02).
stance_target: the correct statistical-significance standard for claiming a search method beats random search/sampling, and the empirical finding that leading NAS methods often fail this test
scope_conditions: PTB language modeling, DARTS/NAO/ENAS search spaces, Welch t-test
quoted_support: ENAS and DARTS cannot be differentiated from the mean of entire search space, while NAO yields worse performance than random sampling.

claim: On CIFAR-10, using the same significance-testing methodology, DARTS does not significantly outperform random sampling (p=0.20), while ENAS and NAO show significant but small improvements (p=0.01 and p=0.00 respectively).
stance_target: the finding that even in the more favorable CNN search space, some leading NAS methods fail to statistically distinguish themselves from random sampling
scope_conditions: CIFAR-10 image classification, DARTS/NAO/ENAS search spaces
quoted_support: While the situation is slightly better in CNN space, all three algorithms still perform similarly to random sampling.

claim: Weight-sharing-derived architecture rankings are essentially uncorrelated with true (from-scratch-trained) architecture rankings in the RNN search space (Kendall tau = -0.004 over 10 runs) and only weakly correlated in the CNN search space (Kendall tau = 0.195), explaining why weight-sharing-based NAS search barely beats random sampling.
stance_target: the mechanistic explanation for why NAS search algorithms using noisy proxy signals fail to reliably beat random baselines -- a rival mechanism to attribute performance parity to, distinct from (but structurally analogous to) unreliable LLM self-generated feedback signals
scope_conditions: reduced/exhaustively-enumerable search spaces, weight-sharing methods, 10 independent runs
quoted_support: the architecture rankings obtained with and without weight sharing are entirely uncorrelated in RNN space (tau = -0.004 over 10 runs); and have little correlation in the CNN space (tau = 0.195 over 10 runs).

claim: In exhaustively-enumerable reduced search spaces, DARTS/NAO/ENAS genuinely fail to discover top-performing architectures, indicating that in some cases the search algorithms' parity with random sampling is not merely because the search space is 'too easy' but reflects a real search-algorithm failure.
stance_target: the finding that parity-with-random-search results cannot always be dismissed as 'the search space did all the work' -- sometimes the algorithm itself is failing to search effectively
quoted_support: we experiment with search spaces where we can exhaustively evaluate all architectures, and observe that these algorithms truly cannot discover top-performing architectures.

claim: Prior random-search baselines in the literature unfairly favored the proposed NAS method: Pham et al. 2018 reports results from only a single random architecture, and Liu et al. 2018 selects the best of only 8 randomly sampled architectures after training for just 300 epochs, whereas a fair comparison requires training all architectures for the full protocol (1000 epochs) and averaging over multiple seeds.
stance_target: the specific historical pattern of under-resourced random-search baselines in NAS papers, which a paper claiming to beat random search must avoid replicating
scope_conditions: citing Pham et al. 2018 (ENAS) and Liu et al. 2018 (DARTS predecessor) baseline setups
quoted_support: Pham et al. 2018 reports the results of only a single random architecture, and Liu et al. 2018b those of an architecture selected among 8 randomly sampled ones as the most promising one after training for 300 epochs only.
numbers: 1000 epochs, multiple seeds (fair comparison used in this paper)

claim: Downstream task results in NAS papers are often reported for only a single random seed, leaving the robustness of search strategies unanswered -- motivating the need to repeat the search itself (not just the final training) across multiple seeds.
stance_target: the requirement for multiple search-phase seeds, distinct from multiple final-training seeds, in a credible NAS comparison
scope_conditions: critique of standard NAS evaluation practice as of 2019
quoted_support: the downstream task results are often reported for a single random seed, which leaves unanswered the question of robustness of the search strategies.
